**The Weight of a Name**

There was a time when names carried more weight than they do now. Not the kind of weight that makes you stumble under their syllables—no, the kind that presses against your ribs, a slow, insistent ache. My name was *Liora*, which means "light" in Hebrew, though no one ever told me that. They just said it like a fact, like the sky was blue or the earth was round. My mother’s voice when she said it was soft, but my father’s was sharp, like a knife testing the edge of a blade. *"Liora,"* he’d say, and I’d flinch, not because he was angry, but because the sound of it was a promise I hadn’t yet broken.

I was twelve when I first understood that names could be weapons. It happened in the schoolyard, where the other girls called me *Liora the Jew* like it was a brand, like it explained everything about me—my hair, my silence, the way I bit my lip when I was nervous. I didn’t know what a Jew was, exactly, only that it was something you weren’t supposed to be if you wanted to fit. So I stopped saying my name. I let them call me *Lior*, short and sharp, like a knife’s first cut. Then *Lia*, softer, easier to swallow. Then nothing at all.

Names are like seeds, my grandmother used to say. Plant them in the right soil, and they grow into something beautiful. Plant them in the wrong soil, and they rot before they take root. She was talking about words, really—how they could heal or wound, how a single syllable could become a home or a cage. I didn’t believe her then. I thought she was just trying to make me feel better about the way my father’s voice still curled around my name like a noose.

But names aren’t just words. They’re the first thing people remember about you. The first thing they forget. The first thing they use to judge you.

I was eighteen when I changed my name for real. Not just to something shorter, but to something entirely new. *Eleanor*. It was my mother’s favorite book character, a girl who wore green and carried a pocket watch and never once let anyone tell her what to do. I took it like a loan, like a secret I was supposed to keep. My father didn’t even notice when I stopped answering to *Liora*. He was too busy yelling about the war, about the checks in the mail, about how the world was ending and there was nothing we could do about it.

Names are like shadows, I realized later. They follow you, even when you try to leave them behind. *Eleanor* didn’t make me lighter. It didn’t make me safer. It just made me someone else’s story for a little while.

I was twenty-five when I went back to *Liora*. Not because I missed it, but because I missed the weight of it. The way it felt to carry something that wasn’t just a name, but a history, a warning, a prayer. I wrote it on my passport. I said it in the mirror. I let my mother’s hands linger on my shoulders when she said it, like she was checking to see if I was still there.

Names are like the earth itself—you can try to dig yourself out of them, but you’ll always be part of the soil. You’ll always be the roots you can’t see.

And sometimes, that’s enough.
